title: Parking Lots & Garages in the US
one_liner: The U.S. parking-lot-and-garage business is a mature, highly fragmented infrastructure service industry that is recovering slowly from post-pandemic demand shocks while accelerating digital parking, mobile payments, and contract-based operating models.
overview: The 2022 IBIS baseline showed this industry in early recovery after the 2020 demand shock, with 2022 revenue estimated at US$7,954m and modest near-term rebound. In 2025-2026, available updates indicate that operators are shifting more value capture to managed contracts, off-street platform-enabled services, and smart-city parking technology (e.g., app payments, reservations, connected-car integrations). Demand support is increasingly cyclical across events, hospitality, and airports, while growth is constrained by high local saturation, ride-hailing substitution risks, and remote/commute pattern changes.

market_size.2025: US$10.3 billion (industry-reported in 2026 parking lots and garages market report summary)

baseline_2022.growth: 2004-2022 CAGR -1.62%; IBIS projected 2022-2028 CAGR 1.07%

how_it_makes_money: Operators earn from hourly, daily, and monthly parking fees, monthly facility-management contracts, valet and auxiliary services, airport and municipal service tenders, and often share-based terms with property owners. Management contracts remain central: operators increasingly scale via long-term fee arrangements rather than owning all facilities, lowering upfront capital exposure while preserving recurring cash flow from throughput and premium services.
cost_structure: Cost structure is labor-intensive, with high fixed operating requirements (attendants, security, enforcement, maintenance, rent/leases, utilities, insurance) and generally low permanent construction intensity when operators run contracted rather than self-owned sites. EBIT margin support depends on utilization, labor productivity, and technology spend: automation, reservation and payment systems raise utilization and reduce leakage, while adding software integration and EV-amenity capex.
major_players: LAZ Parking (national operator; acquired FleetLogix and expanded fleet/truck parking focus in 2025)
SP Plus Corporation (acquired by Metropolis in 2024; became a largest US parking network with >4,000 locations)
ABM Industries (broader facility operator with parking and guest services footprint)
ParkMobile/Arrive (largest private digital parking and mobility provider footprint in North America)
current_dynamics: 2025-2026 dynamics show clear bifurcation: traditional lot/garage pricing remains tied to local land-use and mobility demand, while digital layers (mobile payment, reservations, and data intelligence) are becoming strategic for both operators and cities. Municipal partnerships are increasing, parking is increasingly managed as part of broader urban mobility software stacks, and major events such as the 2026 World Cup are expected to create short-cycle demand spikes in host metros.
whats_growing: Digital channels: in-car payments, reservations, and demand-visibility tools are expanding across city programs and private portfolios.
Management-contract share: operators are pushing managed portfolios where recurring fees reduce capital intensity.
EV readiness at parking facilities: charging infrastructure is becoming a commercial differentiator as EV fleets and commuting patterns evolve.
Event-driven demand: major sports/entertainment cycles (including 2026 FIFA season demand) increase willingness to pay for guaranteed or reserved parking.
whats_shrinking: Pure walk-up dependency in CBDs is pressured by remote work and diversified transport choices.
Standalone ad hoc parking operations without app or reservation enablement are losing pricing power.
Pure spot/price-only growth is limited in saturated urban locations where land-use and new development intensity remains constrained.
recent_developments: 2025-04-22: LAZ Parking acquired a majority stake in FleetLogix, expanding managed parking operations tied to 37 airports and 2,400 employees.
2025-06-24: ParkMobile cited 18% of U.S. adults planning road trips for FIFA 2026 and 70% requiring paid parking among likely attendees.
2025-11-18: ParkMobile announced expansion of parking reservations by approximately 8,000 new U.S. locations via Flash.
2025-11-05: San Francisco launched ParkMobile for >26,000 on-street spaces and began broader municipal integration.
2026-08-03: ParkMobile and Parkopedia announced in-car parking payments in more than 80,000 U.S. locations.
2025-11-14: ParkMobile launched in Buffalo at 4,300 on-street and off-street spaces, adding city-level digital parking analytics.
outlook: The most likely 2026-2028 path is muted top-line growth for physical supply but faster monetization from software-enabled occupancy and pricing controls. Operators that combine contract discipline, dynamic demand tools, and EV-compatible assets should outpace peers, while consolidation is likely to continue among major national and regional operators.
themes: From lot operations to mobility platform economics
Management contracts and lower asset intensity
Smart-city parking integration
Event and airport demand concentration
EV charging as an asset upgrade and retention tool
Industry-level consolidation

title: Party & Event Planners
one_liner: US event-planning demand is steady in 2025–26 but increasingly disciplined, with planners competing on ROI, AI-enabled execution, and premium in-person experiences.
overview: US party and event planning is a small-business-heavy services sector that sits between consumer spending cycles and corporate budget discipline. Demand is still resilient, especially for weddings and high-stakes corporate events, but planners face rising execution costs, shorter planning cycles, and stronger scrutiny of outcomes; this is accelerating hybrid-ready workflows and software-enabled planning.

market_size.party_and_event_planning: $3.2 billion (2022 estimate used as 2022 baseline from IBISWorld-cited industry summaries)

key_stats.growth: Party/event summaries cite -0.3% CAGR in 2018-2023 and modest 2022 recovery, while Trade Show & Event Planning shows +12.8% CAGR in 2021-2026; wedding services show +6.8% CAGR in 2025-2030; wedding event spending rose +8.5% YoY through May 2026.

baseline_2022.growth: 2022 had recovery from prior years (reported around +4% YoY in cited IBISWorld-based summaries; broader party/event historical period still weak)

how_it_makes_money: Primary revenue comes from planning/coordination retainers, milestone-based project fees, producer markups on vendor contracts, ticketing and registration service fees, attendee management packages, and add-on services (AV, destination logistics, staffing, and post-event analytics).
cost_structure: Most costs are labor and payroll, subcontractor/vendor payments, venue and catering commitments, travel/logistics, insurance and compliance, marketing leads/acquisition, and technology subscriptions (registration, planning, ticketing, and analytics tools).
current_dynamics: Corporate planners are becoming ROI-first and selective: budgets are improving in some quarters but are constrained by inflation and attendance uncertainty. AI use is accelerating in planning workflows, yet planners still report uneven confidence in using it for memorable experiences, and in-person attendance remains a core objective while virtual is used tactically.
whats_growing: Event professionals using generative AI regularly climbed to 70% in Q1 2026
Wedding demand remains resilient, with ~2M US marriages in 2025 and >$100B total wedding spending
Intentional/experience-led event design is gaining importance (high share of professionals call it essential)
Corporate event buyers are returning to in-person planning but with tighter scope control and stronger value requirements
Software-led coordination (registration, workflow automation, attendee data) is expanding in the US event stack
whats_shrinking: Perceived budget freedom for non-essential event line items is shrinking as costs rise
Average meeting format is becoming more selective and shorter in planning horizon
ROI skepticism is reducing tolerance for expensive 'nice-to-have' experiences
Some multinational and cross-border meeting activity is being reduced or reconfigured due to costs/uncertainty
recent_developments: 2026-06-30: Bank of America Institute reported wedding-related spending +8.5% YoY and ~2M marriages in 2025 with >$100B total wedding event spend.
2026-Q1: MPI Meetings Outlook showed AI regular use rising to 70% (from 22% in Q4 2023), with sentiment still generally positive but less uniformly optimistic.
2026-Q2: MPI Q2 Outlook described a squeeze from rising production costs and higher scrutiny on event value, with more right-sizing and line-by-line budget pressure.
2026-Q3: MPI reported 56% of respondents expecting favorable budgets and 61% seeing live attendance as a positive planning factor.

2026-05-08: Skift cited 57% of event professionals expecting favorable conditions and 53% expecting flat-to-positive budgets, while geopolitical and travel constraints still pressure planning choices.
outlook: Near-term industry momentum is moderate but not fragile: event demand is steady into 2026, while margin risk is rising. Leaders that combine disciplined budgeting, stronger pre/post-event analytics, and hybrid operational capabilities should gain share; price-sensitive segments are likely to see fragmentation and specialization rather than broad expansion.
themes: AI integration as productivity layer
Outcome-first/ROI-driven event procurement
Premium in-person experience versus cost pressure
Wedding sector resilience despite macro inflation
Geopolitical, travel, and compliance complexity driving format mix
one_sentence: Party and event planning in 2026 remains tied to discretionary spend, with weddings and corporate events driving most activity while buyers demand tighter economics and measurable outcomes.

title: Party Supply Rental
one_liner: Party supply rental is a fragmented local service market where event gear rental is increasingly bundled with setup and planning services to capture higher margins.
overview: The industry rents tables, chairs, tents, linens, audio, tables-and-chairs sets, and specialty décor and support products for social events and business functions. Demand is event-driven and seasonally concentrated, with stronger activity in spring through fall and peak wedding periods. While rental transactions remain core, operators increasingly differentiate with delivery, setup, event consultations, and design support to reduce price-only competition. The market is fragmented, with limited national concentration and many regional operators.

key_stats.market_size: US $8.5 billion (2026)
key_stats.growth: 4.0% CAGR (2021-2026, IBISWorld basis)
key_stats.trade_show_proxy: Trade Show & Event Planning market $24.7 billion in 2026

baseline_2022.market_size: $4.96 billion (2022 modeled from 2021 baseline and 2021-2026 growth path)
baseline_2022.growth: about 5.1% annualized in baseline projection path

how_it_makes_money: Primary revenue is short-duration rental of event equipment (tables, chairs, tents, tablescape items, audio/lighting and decor). Secondary revenue comes from delivery and pickup fees, setup/teardown labor, consultation and styling, consultation-led bundles, and upsells into adjacent services for weddings and corporate events.

cost_structure.inventory_cost: Large upfront capital for durable goods and replacement/repair cycles as units wear, are stained, or become obsolete.
cost_structure.labour: Crew scheduling for delivery, setup, teardown, pickup, and event-day support; seasonal hiring pressure increases labor cost volatility.
cost_structure.storage_and_transport: Warehouse/garage footprint, fleet fuel insurance, routing, and maintenance are significant fixed and variable expenses.
cost_structure.customer_acquisition: Digital search, social platforms, and referral channels are major marketing expense lines, especially in peak planning periods.
cost_structure.liability_and_compliance: Insurance coverage, licenses, and safety/compliance obligations are required to access premium venues and corporate accounts.

current_dynamics: Demand is recovering in line with discretionary spend and event revival, with weddings and social ceremonies still a major stabilizer. Corporate event demand is supported by stronger B2B exhibition and conference activity, while operators are investing in service layers to escape commoditization. Digital planning behavior and AI usage among event planners and couples is increasing, pushing digital lead capture and faster response expectations.
whats_growing: Wedding volume remained high in 2025 with an estimated 2.0 million U.S. marriages, keeping event décor and rental demand resilient.
B2B exhibition demand signals are improving, with IAEE noting stronger attendance, exhibitor participation, and forward bookings in 2025 through the 2026 CEIR outlook.
Value-added service demand (setup, styling, planning support) is rising as operators shift away from pure price competition.
Consolidation activity is visible through small-to-midsize acquisition activity in the event-rental niche.
AI and planning automation adoption is rising in consumer-facing event planning workflows.
whats_shrinking: Pure commodity rental pricing is under pressure as consumers compare online and local offers.
Revenue concentration remains seasonal, with pronounced peaks and weaker utilization in winter months.
Skilled-event-staffing is constrained, increasing operational risk around peak weekends.
International travel uncertainty can suppress large trade-show driven corporate demand in some segments.
recent_developments: 2025-01: The Knot Worldwide reported 2025 wedding research showing enduring ceremony demand, with 2.0 million U.S. marriages and high vendorized event spending.
2025-08: The Knot Worldwide released its 2025 future-of-celebrations reporting, reinforcing trend-based spending resilience around life-events.
2026-02: The Knot 2026 Real Weddings Study showed average U.S. wedding cost at $34,000 in 2025, with 2.0 million weddings, signaling continued core demand for rental-supported ceremonies.
2026-04: PCMA published the 2026 Outlook framework, citing more selective, outcome-driven event spending and format shifts in corporate programming.
2026-05: IAEE released the 2026 CEIR Index and forecast notes, citing improving B2B exhibition fundamentals and forward-booking strength.
2026-07: Curated Events announced the acquisition of Montana Party Rentals, consistent with ongoing consolidation in event rental providers.
outlook: Near-term market expansion should remain moderate into 2026, driven by resilient weddings and recovering corporate events, but pricing remains weak at the commodity level. Winners are likely operators that combine broad inventory depth with reliable logistics and event-service bundles, while fragmented independent operators remain vulnerable to labor and utilization swings. Expect slow concentration around better-capitalized regional networks.
themes: Service-led differentiation over pure rental
Seasonality management through weddings plus corporate/event hybrid mix
Digital booking and AI-assisted planning
Consolidation and portfolio-style local-to-national operating models
Inventory uptime and logistics reliability as trust differentiators
one_sentence: The U.S. party supply rental market has rebounded from pandemic disruption into a moderate-growth, highly competitive services industry tied to weddings and corporate events.

title: Pasta Sauce Production
one_liner: A mature U.S. packaged pasta-sauce manufacturing category with slow growth, strong price competition, and faster demand shifts toward cleaner-label premium formats.
overview: U.S. pasta sauce production covers tomato, cream, and vegetable/oil-based sauces used in households and foodservice. The industry is mature with low organic growth, fragmented competition, and high import rivalry, while input exposure remains tied to processed tomato supply and household health preferences. Baseline IBIS data shows revenue around USD 6.262 billion in 2022; the long-run category path is only slightly positive through 2027.

key_stats.market_size: USD 6,262 million in 2022 (IBIS baseline); USD 6,389 million estimated in 2026 using the IBIS 2022-2027 trajectory
key_stats.growth: 0.44% CAGR projected for 2022-2028; 2022 revenue changed -0.1%.

baseline_2022.growth: -1.4% CAGR over prior five years; approximately -0.1% in 2022.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers sell branded and private-label sauces through grocery retailers, supermarkets, wholesalers, and foodservice channels, mainly in shelf-stable formats (jar, can, pouch) with promotions, category innovation, and flavor extensions for margin and share gains. Core revenue drivers are volume from FAH channels and mix upgrades to premium/health-oriented SKUs.

cost_structure.raw_materials: Tomato processing, oils, dairy (for cream variants), sugar, herbs, and packaging ingredients are primary variable costs; USDA reported U.S. processing tomatoes at 11.6 million tons in 2025 (+5% y/y).
cost_structure.import_exposure: U.S. was a net importer of tomato sauce in 2025, increasing competitive pressure from imports; Italy supplied 83% of imported sauce volume.
cost_structure.labor_and_ops: Labor and operating efficiency remain sensitive to wage pressure and fulfillment/marketing costs, especially with retail and foodservice distribution.
cost_structure.pricing_pressure: Food-at-home inflation (2.3% in 2025) is moderate, so producers compete on shelf differentiation and private-label response as premium inflation tails off in categories.

current_dynamics: Demand is bifurcating: households with stronger away-from-home spending (FAFH share 56.3% of total food spending in 2025) pressure home-cook sauce refresh cycles, while stronger tomato-processing supply (11.6 million tons processed tomatoes in 2025) and high imported sauce penetration (676.7M pounds in 2025) keep margins and pricing under pressure.
whats_growing: Premium and clean-label reformulations are the strongest growth pockets
Foodservice-linked demand remains supported as restaurant recovery continues in 2026
Brand-level innovation is active; Rao’s and Prego are gaining in-unit/brand value in recent earnings updates
whats_shrinking: Broad-volume conventional formats are pressured by wellness and label transparency preferences
Import competition in tomato-sauce categories is rising, especially from Italy at 83% of 2025 imported sauce volume
recent_developments: 2026-03: IMARC reported U.S. pasta-sauce market size of USD 2.6 billion in 2025 and USD 3.1 billion forecast by 2034 (market estimate update).
2026-03: USDA ERS reported U.S. processed tomato production in 2025 at 11.6 million tons, up 5% from 2024.
2026-03-20: USDA ERS Vegetables and Pulses Outlook stated Italy supplied 83% of U.S. imported tomato sauce volume in 2025 (676.7 million lbs, fresh-weight equivalent basis 2.2 billion lbs).
2026-06: NRA expected U.S. restaurant and foodservice sales to rise 4.3% in 2026.
2026-06: Campbell Soup Q2 FY26 reported Rao’s exceeded USD 1B in trailing twelve-month net sales and 11.5% sauce consumption growth in the quarter.
2026-07: Campbell Soup Q3 FY26 reported Rao’s drove 75% of total sauce category growth and Prego retained #1 unit share.
outlook: 2026-2027 is likely a slow-growth period: category growth remains limited, but branded leaders should capture share through premium variants and stronger execution in grocery and foodservice placements; value likely remains relatively stable with continued consolidation.
themes: Health-conscious reformulation (low sugar, lower sodium, cleaner labels)
Convenience-oriented at-home use and pantry resilience
Foodservice rebound + blended demand between FAFH and FAH
Competitive pressure from imports and private label
Premiumization through regional, organic, and fusion-style flavors
one_sentence: By 2026 the category is stable in value but selective in growth, supported by convenience demand and foodservice recovery while conventional, higher-sodium formats lose share to wellness-driven alternatives.

title: Paving Contractors in the US
one_liner: The U.S. paving-contractor industry is a small, maintenance-heavy segment led by driveway and parking-lot work, with growth tied to residential activity and constrained by high input costs.
overview: The industry covers driveway and parking-area paving for commercial and residential customers, plus sealcoating, striping, and repairs. The segment is mature and fragmented, with 2022 IBIS data already showing modest volume growth and structurally low barriers to entry. In the 2026 Top 40 contractor set, the mix stayed maintenance-led (80% existing pavement, 20% new work), confirming that recurring service activity is the core engine of revenue and profit durability.

market_size.2026_specialized_segment_reference: 2026 Top 40 Paving Contractors reported US$1.278B in total gross sales and US$638.5M in paving-only sales

growth.2022_2027_top40_proxy: Top 40 paving-only remained resilient on a per-contractor basis (US$15.96M avg. per contractor) while total pool stayed soft

2022_segment_mix_reference.paving_mix_2026_top40_avg: Paving 49.4%, sealcoating 15.6%, pavement repair 15.3%, striping 5.7%, other 12.8%

primary_revenue: Driveways (including residential and smaller private projects)
Maintenance-driven repair work, sealcoating, and striping
how_it_makes_money.pricing_structure: Contractors price by project scope and material system (asphalt vs concrete/pavers), with custom surfaces and municipal/commercial specifications creating premium tiers.
how_it_makes_money.revenue_diversity_note: In 2026 Top 40 data, driveway work rose to 13.4% from 11.6% and parking lots remained near 61.0%, while highway work was only 3.5%.

cost_structure.labor: Paving/surfacing operator wage pressure remains meaningful; BLS occupational data (2025 release) shows paving, surfacing, and tamping equipment operators at US$59,000 annual mean wage, 41,820 employees nationally in that occupation.
cost_structure.materials: Asphalt paving mixture PPI was elevated and volatile: FRED WPU13940113C reported Jun 2026 = 159.520 (Index Dec 2009=100), versus Mar 2026 = 174.208.
cost_structure.fuel_equipment: Fleet replacement is capital intensive; 70% of Top 40 operators reported equipment spending above US$2M in 2026.
cost_structure.financing_sensitivity: Mortgage-rate environment affects residential lead demand indirectly; 30-year FRM averaged 6.30% on 2026-04-30 (Freddie Mac PMMS), above 2025 pre-peak levels.
cost_structure.margin_context: Top 40 2026 margin-band concentration remained in upper tiers (62.5% above 16%) despite some redistribution from >20% into 16–20% bucket.

current_dynamics.demand_mix: Residential-led demand remains visible (2025 starts were 1,358,700 units and Dec-2025 starts were 1,404,000 SAAR), while monthly housing construction activity still showed softening versus prior-year levels.
current_dynamics.construction_market_context: Census private construction spending remained relatively flat to weak in parts: March 2026 private nonresidential at US$729.4B and residential at US$929.7B SAAR; May 2026 private nonresidential at US$738.7B and residential at US$930.2B SAAR.
current_dynamics.pricing_and_cost: Asphalt-price input inflation has been uneven: WPU13940113C climbed from Apr-2026 153.281 to Jun-2026 159.520, with a prior March correction to 174.208, indicating high input volatility.
current_dynamics.segment_behavior: The Top 40 contractor set confirms a durable service cycle: 80% of completed work on maintenance and only 20% on new surface, reducing dependence on major capital cycles in any single month.

whats_growing: Maintenance-led demand and repair/repeat-customer retention in the Top 40 data (55% of contractors doing >400 projects).
Share of single-family-oriented commercial-residential crossover work in Top 40 customers and mix (single-family mix rose to 13.1%).
Project mix moving toward driveway-oriented residential work (13.4% in Top 40), supporting smaller-batch service delivery.
whats_shrinking: Top-40 total gross scale remains below prior-year Top 50 aggregate context, even as per-contractor paving productivity improved.
New-construction dependence remains capped by unchanged 20% share of work; highway work stays low (3.5%).
Aggregate demand sensitivity persists from rate-sensitive housing and construction-cost inflation; mortgage and input cost headwinds are structural.
recent_developments: 2026-07-15: US paving mixtures PPI (WPU13940113C) recorded 159.520 (Jun 2026, Dec 2009=100) on FRED.
2026-07-01: Census Monthly Construction Spending (May 2026) showed total $2,210.2B SAAR, private $1,669.0B, residential $930.2B, nonresidential $738.7B, public $541.2B.
2026-06-12: Top 40 Paving Contractors report showed paving-only revenue of $638.5M, total Top 40 gross $1.278B, with 80% maintenance / 20% new construction.
2026-04-30: Freddie Mac PMMS reported a 30-year fixed FRM of 6.30% in the U.S.
2026-02-18: Census Dec-2025 new residential construction release reported housing starts 1,404,000 SAAR and annual 2025 starts 1,358,700 units.
outlook: For 2026–2027, the sector likely remains in a constrained-growth posture: durable maintenance demand should hold baseline volume while new-construction upside is limited by high financing rates and muted broad nonresidential pace. With pavement lifecycle cycles and repeat-maintenance work dominant, profitability depends on fleet efficiency, pricing discipline, and material purchasing strategy rather than large one-off expansion.
themes: Maintenance-first demand model
Residential pivot in mix (single-family and driveway-oriented work rising)
Input-cost volatility (asphalt/paving materials, fuel, and equipment) compressing margins
Consolidation by capability rather than dominance: more operators above threshold margins but no single large national concentration
Execution leverage through repeat municipal/commercial relationships
one_sentence: US paving contractors are shifting to a model where existing-surface maintenance dominates, while new-construction work remains secondary and margin stability depends on productivity, asphalt supply costs, and residential demand.

title: Pawn Shops
one_liner: Pawn shops are a niche short-term credit and resale model: small, non-recourse collateral loans plus buy/sell of used personal goods, with industry cash-flow now increasingly driven by large multi-country operators.
overview: Pawn shops serve underbanked and credit-constrained households through pledged-collateral loans and inventory-based retail sales. The sector combines lending and second-hand commerce, with demand influenced by disposable income, access to bank credit, and household liquidity stress. The largest operator remains an integrated network model (FirstCash), while independent operators remain active and highly fragmented, making competitive dynamics dependent on location density, real estate ownership, and underwriting discipline.

key_stats.market_size: ~$3.0 billion (NPA cites IBISWorld, Sep 2024), with 7,771 U.S. stores
key_stats.growth: IBIS trend: -1.3% annualized projected 2021-2026; however, major operators reported growth in 2025 and early 2026
key_stats.unemployment_context: U.S. CPI/Wage pressure with 2026 labor backdrop: U.S. unemployment 4.1% in Jul 2026 (CPS)

baseline_2022.market_size: $2,936 million (IBISWorld historical baseline referenced in 2021/2026 outlook context)
baseline_2022.growth: -1.67% CAGR (2005-2021 historical; pre-2022 decline context)

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is primarily from pawn loan service fees (non-recourse, collateral-backed credit) and retail merchandise sales from forfeited/consigned goods; FirstCash disclosed pawn fees around 46% and pawn merchandise gross-profit share around 39% of consolidated net revenue in 2025, while pawn loan fees in its network are commonly in the 4%-25% monthly range by collateral type. Supplemental revenue in the U.S. retail POS segment is lease-to-own transaction support and related payment solutions.
cost_structure: Largest cost elements are labor, occupancy, store operations (security/insurance/ utilities), treasury and credit funding costs, depreciation/amortization, interest expense, and regulatory/compliance overhead; in SEC filings FirstCash highlights store-level payroll, occupancy, bank/treasury fees, security, and IT as core pawn operating costs.
major_players: FirstCash Holdings (global leader, over 3,300 pawn stores globally, 1,207 U.S. stores as of Mar 2026)
EZCORP (1,360 total locations as of Sep 30, 2025; second largest U.S. pawn operator)
Numerous independent and small multi-store operators, with industry described as highly fragmented outside top operators
current_dynamics: FirstCash and peers are reporting sustained loan-demand acceleration and robust same-store receivables growth through early 2026, while also deepening footprint via openings and acquisitions across U.S., Latin America and U.K.; regulatory and labor variables (minimum wage in Mexico, interest rates, and compliance scope) remain active cost and margin sensitivities. Growth is strongest in networks with scale, stronger real-estate control, and direct integration of acquired locations.
whats_growing: 2025-11-13: EZCORP reported 1,360 total locations (545 U.S., 622 Mexico, 193 Central America) in 2025.
2025-12-31: FirstCash reported 3,330 pawn locations after adding 344 stores in 2025.
2026-02-05: FirstCash reported record Q4 2025 results with 2025 full-year revenue $3,661 million and 2025 net income $330 million.
2026-03-31: FirstCash operated 3,334 pawn locations and reported 2026 Q1 consolidated revenue of $1,051.651 million.
2026-04-23: FirstCash raised 2026 guidance for pawn segment revenues after Q1 same-store pawn receivables up 19% U.S., 30% LatAm, 29% U.K. (local currency).
2026-12-15: Fed/CFR threshold update for Truth in Lending and consumer leasing moved dollar thresholds for 2026, affecting some subprime/consumer credit products.
whats_shrinking: Industry-level contraction signal remains in historical IBIS framing (declining establishments/enterprises over prior years).
Consolidation pressure means local independents are being outcompeted by integrated chains with stronger sourcing, analytics and financing infrastructure.
Banks and fintech alternatives remain a structural substitute where credit access improves, capping growth of low-margin first-time borrowings in improving macro pockets.
recent_developments: 2025-11-13 (EZCORP FY2025): reported 1,360 total pawn locations and continued operating growth in Mexico, including continued focus on pawn service charges and scrap/jewelry economics.
2026-02-05 (FirstCash 2025 full-year/FQ4): announced 12% full-year U.S. segment growth and raised 2026 confidence with 344 stores added in 2025 to 3,330 total.
2026-04-23 (FirstCash Q1 2026): reported 26% consolidated revenue growth, Q1 net income up 29%, and new store count of 3,334 with raised 2026 guidance.
2026-07-22 (SEC filing activity): company disclosed ongoing growth and balance-sheet management while maintaining high capital intensity in expansion and real-estate ownership.
2026-08-07 (BLS CPS): U.S. unemployment was 4.1% in Jul 2026, supporting demand stabilization in low-income credit-need households.
2026-12-15 (Federal Reserve): consumer-culture credit threshold updates under Reg Z/Reg M signal tighter documentation and compliance visibility in small-dollar credit markets.
outlook: Near term, operator-level earnings momentum looks strong through 2026, especially for platform operators adding scale, while broader industry health is tied to household credit stress versus wage gains and bank-credit inclusion. Over the medium term, expect continued consolidation, greater cross-market integration (including LatAm and U.K.), and persistent debate over small-dollar lending terms and digital onboarding standards.
themes: Counter-cyclical demand with resilience at low-income income levels
Dual-model economics: secured lending + resale of used goods
Consolidation and platformization
Cross-border growth in LatAm as a hedge to U.S. volatility
Regulation and compliance rising in importance for small-dollar credit
one_sentence: U.S. pawn operations grew sharply in 2025-2026 at the operator level despite earlier sector-level contraction forecasts, with major roll-ups expanding scale and margin leverage.

title: Payroll & Bookkeeping Services in the US
one_liner: US payroll-and-bookkeeping remains a mid-single-digit, AI-accelerating outsourcing market anchored by payroll tax compliance complexity and SMB digitization, with large HCM platforms consolidating share while smaller local operators still retain a long tail.
overview: The US market is defined by outsourced payroll, tax filing, benefits/payroll tax administration, and bookkeeping workflow support for small and mid-market businesses. The 2022 IBIS benchmark positioned the sector at USD 61.8bn in revenue and projected it to rise toward USD 68.2bn by 2027 (about 2% annualized growth). In 2025-2026, public platform providers report resilient growth—ADP, Intuit, and Paycom all reported strong FY2025 results with multi-year pricing/booking momentum, while major acquirers signaled further consolidation (for example, Paychex–Paycor). AI and automation are increasing service stickiness in payroll and payroll-linked accounting, yet margins remain sensitive to labor/insurance costs, compliance complexity, and financing conditions for SMB clients.

small_business_context.job_change_2024_to_2025_monthly_report_s: 51,200 jobs lost; avg revenue per small business down $11,850 in Intuit small-business sample

how_it_makes_money: Recurring payroll processing subscriptions (small-business and enterprise payroll engines),
HCM/HR automation, onboarding, and workforce management workflows embedded in payroll platforms (ADP, Intuit, Paycom, Paychex/Ceridian ecosystems),
Payroll tax filing and compliance services (state/federal remittance, W-2/W-4/1099 workflows),
PEO/HR outsourcing contracts where payroll, workers’ compensation, and unemployment tax administration are bundled,
Interest income on client funds held in trust-like cash balances (material for ADP scale),
Add-on modules such as payroll tax credits, benefits administration, payments, and AI copilots for bookkeeping/tax support.
cost_structure: Employee-intensive implementation, support, and managed services (high share of cost base across providers),
Compliance and audit-related operating complexity (updates for changing federal/state payroll rules),
Insurance and worker-related costs in PEO models, including workers’ compensation and unemployment exposures,
Technology platform spend (R&D and cloud delivery, payroll security, AI features),
Selling and marketing/partner distribution for SMB acquisition and retention,
M&A-related integration and restructuring costs (notably active in 2025-2026 deals),
Interest-rate-sensitive investment income and liability management on client payroll-held funds.
current_dynamics: 2026-01-28: ADP reported fiscal Q2 FY26 revenue up 6% to $5.4bn and raised FY26 outlook; EPS and EBIT both up 10%.
2026-04-29: ADP reported fiscal Q3 FY26 revenue up 7% to $5.9bn and again raised FY26 outlook.
2025-10-29: ADP FY26 initial outlook set total revenue growth at 5%-6% and PEO revenue growth 5%-7% with rising average worksite employees.
2025-08-21: Intuit reported FY25 total revenue up 16% to $18.8bn and gave FY26 guidance of $20.997bn-$21.186bn (about +12% to +13%).
2025-01-14: Intuit small-business index reported 2024 small-business stress signs (51,200 job decline, avg revenue down $11,850), reinforcing demand for reliable payroll/compliance services.
2025-01/2026: Paycom launched AI payroll solution IWant™ and guided 2026 total revenue to $2.175bn-$2.195bn (6%-7% growth).
2025-04-14: Paychex finalized acquisition of Paycor (~$4.1bn purchase value), signaling continued payroll-services consolidation.
whats_growing: ADoption of AI-enabled payroll and bookkeeping features in SMB workflows (documented by major providers and product launches).
Outsourcers expanding beyond payroll into full HCM/benefits/payments bundles to raise switching costs.
Cross-selling within integrated ecosystems (payroll + tax + bookkeeping + lending/payments).
Consolidation pace: Paychex+Paycor and ongoing integration behavior by the top platforms.
whats_shrinking: SMB revenue resilience is mixed: Intuit’s 2024-2025 small-business sample showed higher average debt burden and revenue weakness despite partial recovery, which can constrain spend on non-core finance functions.
Margins in PEO/managed payroll models face pressure from insurance and payroll-admin cost inflation.
Price compression risk for low-complexity, low-touch payroll-only offerings as enterprises/SMBs compare against fully integrated stacks.
recent_developments: 2025-01-14: Intuit Small Business Index reported 51,200 small-business jobs down and average revenue per business down $11,850.
2025-08-21: Intuit reported FY25 revenue +16% to $18.8bn and gave FY26 guidance $20.997bn-$21.186bn.
2025-10-29: ADP FY26 Q1 release showed 7% revenue growth ($5.2bn) and reiterated full-year FY26 outlook 5%-6%.
2026-01-28: ADP FY26 Q2 results: revenue +6% to $5.4bn and raised FY26 outlook.
2026-04-29: ADP FY26 Q3 results: revenue +7% to $5.9bn and raised FY26 outlook further.
2026-01-30: Paycom launched AI product IWant™ in FY2025 and guided 2026 total revenue to $2.175bn-$2.195bn.
outlook: Near-term outlook is still constructive: major providers project continued low-to-mid single-digit industry pull-through from SMB and mid-market payroll demand, with high client acquisition activity and AI-enabled workflow differentiation. However, industry growth is unlikely to accelerate without broader hiring strength; the key inflection remains whether SMB credit quality and labor demand support sustained software spend. 2026 remains a year of execution on integration and compliance automation, while consolidated balance-sheet strength and deal activity (notably Paychex–Paycor) suggest continued concentration at the top.
themes: AI and automation as a service-level differentiator for accuracy, onboarding, and exception handling.
Platformization: payroll now sold as part of broader workforce and finance ecosystems.
Consolidation pressure in the middle market (acquirers targeting scale and distribution).
Margin discipline: providers balancing growth with insurance, labor, and compliance overhead.
Reliance on macro-financial health of SMBs for new-client growth and pricing power.
one_sentence: Demand is still growing, but 2025-2026 results show competition on platform depth, compliance reliability, and pricing as the market shifts toward integrated AI-driven payroll-finance stacks.

title: Peanut Butter Production
one_liner: US peanut butter production is a durable, branded food category where modest demand growth is offset by volatile raw peanut economics and tighter international supply rules.
overview: U.S. peanut butter production is anchored by high-volume national brands and private-label programs that distribute through grocery retail and foodservice channels. USDA data show a record US peanut crop of 7.2 billion pounds in MY 2025/26 and above-normal peanut inventories, supporting processing throughput even as peanut butter’s category demand was reported weaker than the broader 10-year pattern in 2025/26. The category remains heavily concentrated around major packaged-food operators, but the channel mix is gradually shifting toward health- and convenience-driven variants.

key_stats.market_size: US$2.1 billion (industry-scale, 2026 proxy from 2020 baseline and subsequent trajectory)
key_stats.growth: about +0.9% CAGR from 2022 to 2026
key_stats.raw_input: US peanut production 7.2 billion pounds in MY 2025/26 (record high)
key_stats.food_use: US peanut food use forecast 3.1 billion pounds in MY 2025/26
key_stats.exports: USDA forecast 1.3 billion pounds of peanut exports in MY 2025/26 (revised from 1.5 billion pounds in Sept 2025 outlook)
key_stats.market_share: Peanut butter is the largest U.S. peanut food-use category and accounted for more than 60% of total edible peanut food use

baseline_2022.growth: +0.96% CAGR (derived from 2020–2026 industry trend and industry baseline trajectory)

how_it_makes_money: Selling branded and private-label peanut butter under high-velocity SKUs to grocery and mass merchandisers.
Generating higher-margin volume from multi-jar formats, spread formats, and flavor/texture variants that lift basket size.
Leveraging brand equity and distribution breadth to secure shelf presence, shelf reset, and seasonal promotions.
Earning value from peanut butter and nearby nut-butter/spread line extensions and foodservice substitutions.
cost_structure: Raw shelled peanuts are the largest variable cost and are exposed to year-to-year supply and quality variability.
Refining, roasting, grinding, blending, and packaging conversion costs are high but increasingly automated.
Freight and storage become significant as production and raw input volatility increase year-to-year.
Quality and compliance costs are non-trivial due to aflatoxin and import/traceability standards.
major_players: Post Consumer Brands / Post Holdings (Peter Pan)
National and regional private-label manufacturers (private brands across major retailers)
current_dynamics: US production is strong but category economics remain mixed: 2025/26 showed record peanut supply and higher stocks while peanut butter consumption strength was softer than prior-year food-use momentum, and exports are affected by quality/trade constraints despite continued global demand for U.S. brands.
whats_growing: Peanut butter remains the core US peanut-use category, with sustained share of total peanut food consumption.
Health-positioning tied to protein and convenience is supporting portfolio refreshes.
Private-label and value-tier distribution continues to gain in mature channels.
Brand innovation around flavor/texture and ingredient simplification.
whats_shrinking: Peanut candy share is weaker versus peanut butter in US use composition.
Peanut butter share within total food use has shown a short-term softness in 2025/26 versus the prior-year peak path.
Export upside has been uneven due to stricter quality controls and quota/trade administration.
recent_developments: 2025-09-16: USDA OCS-25I (Sept 2025) forecast peanut food use up 1% in MY 2025/26 to 3,175 million pounds and exports at 1.5 billion pounds.
2025-12-29: USDA NASS released November 2025 Peanut Stocks and Processing tables with category-level peanut butter utilization data and inventory tracking.
2026-01-02: CBP quota bulletin QB 26-211 posted with US quota period Jan 1–Dec 31, 2026 and opening-time entry rules for Peanut Butter and Paste.
2026-02-12: USDA OCS-26b (Feb 2026) reported MY 2025/26 production at 7.2 billion pounds (11% above prior year), but peanut butter consumption down 4% and exports forecast cut to 1.3 billion pounds.
2026-04-14: USDA ERS chart update noted U.S. peanut butter as the dominant consumption category and up 6% versus the prior 10-year average.
outlook: Near term, capacity remains adequate and the category should stay structurally stable, but margin resilience will depend on raw peanut quality, procurement economics, and mix shifts toward higher-value SKUs. US exporters face a dual effect: expanding supply in some destination channels versus softer access in quality-constrained regions. Expect gradual recovery in blended demand quality via premium, clean-label, and protein-oriented positioning rather than broad unit expansion.
themes: Supply scale and stock volatility management
Brand concentration vs private-label pressure
Health/nutrition-led reformulation
Trade administration and quota complexity for imports
Automation to offset commodity and labor cost pressure
one_sentence: The US industry stays near a $2 billion scale in 2025–2026 with high brand concentration, strong peanut-crop throughput, and mixed growth as peanut butter demand holds while some adjacent peanut categories soften.

title: Peer-to-Peer Lending Platforms
one_liner: U.S. peer-to-peer and marketplace lending is rebounding from a rate-cycle slowdown into a faster, more institutional and platform-centered credit model.
overview: The U.S. marketplace lending base is shifting from pure originator-driven growth toward bank-connected and institutional-capital-backed distribution. Public operators reported accelerating 2025–2026 credit throughput, with LendingClub guiding full-year 2026 loan originations to $11.6–$12.6 billion and Prosper delivering 11 percent-plus annualized Q1 2026 growth in consumer originations. Regulatory activity in late 2025 and 2026 (Section 1071 and ECOA implementation updates) is a major constraint on expansion, even as lenders build stronger AI and servicing economics.

growth.lendingclub_q1_2026_vs_guidance_percent: 31% annualized growth in Q1 versus 2025 comparable period on reported trajectory

market_size.method: estimated using largest-public-marketplace-originator proxy (Prosper + LendingClub listed platform originations)

how_it_makes_money: Origination fees paid by borrowers on funded loans
Servicing fees and collections-related fees from loan servicing operations
Net interest spread and credit income on loans retained on balance sheet (where licensed as bank or finance entities)
Change in fair value and trading/derivative gains on loan portfolios as relevant
Investor/platform referral and partner origination fees for fee-based loan-platform business
cost_structure: Technology and compliance stack (AI underwriting, fraud, anti-fraud, KYC/AML, data, and model governance)
Credit risk allowance and provisioning under higher-rate and macro-volatility conditions
Sales, marketing, and acquisition CAC as platforms compete with banks and card products
Servicing infrastructure and third-party partner management (especially platform and loan-pipeline partnerships)
Legal and regulatory reporting burden tied to small-business and consumer-credit oversight

current_dynamics: The 2025–2026 cycle is characterized by stronger platformization: lenders increasingly monetize borrower sourcing and servicing rather than only principal growth. AI-assisted underwriting and automation are becoming core cost advantages (notably LendingClub’s >90% issued-loan automation claim), while lenders that secure durable institutional commitments (SoFi LPB, loan commitments and partner funding lines) reduce balance-sheet intensity.
whats_growing: Institutional and partner-sourced capital commitments for loan-platform businesses
AI workflow penetration in underwriting, pricing, collections routing, and servicing operations
Fee-based partnership models that shift activity from direct balance-sheet dependence to platform fees
whats_shrinking: Pure marketplace revenue sensitivity in periods of higher-for-longer interest rates and tighter underwriting pullback
Standalone margin at some retail-facing origination channels as investors demand higher yield and risk controls tighten
recent_developments: 2025-11-13: CFPB issued a proposed reconsideration of Section 1071 small-business lending rules (Coverage, small-business definition, and data-point changes).

outlook: Near-term growth is likely but uneven: stronger demand and partnership-led throughput should support volume, while regulatory revision cycles, credit-cycle uncertainty, and compliance economics are likely to pressure margins. Platforms that are most efficient in automation and partnerships should gain share even as consumer-direct marketplace lending remains selective.

title: Performers & Creative Artists in the US
one_liner: A large, fragmented creative economy where independent operators dominate and platforms, licensing, and subscriptions are the primary modern revenue channels.
overview: The industry remains dominated by independent creators and freelancers, with many operators working as sole proprietors and combining multiple revenue streams. Demand is increasingly routed through digital channels and recurring models, while traditional live-program spending and public arts grants remain important but comparatively cyclical and budget-sensitive.

market_size.2026_recorded_music_anchor: US$11.5bn (US recorded music market in 2025, reported March 16, 2026 by RIAA)
market_size.nonemployer_activity_anchor_2023: 1,043,306 individual proprietorships and US$25.4bn receipts in NAICS 711510 as reported in 2023 nonemployer-based figures (latest public breakdown referenced by Census article)
market_size.payroll_scale_anchor_2026: NAICS 7115 nonfarm payroll employees at 56.3k in May 2026 (BLS CES)

growth.music_revenue: +recorded music growth implied by 2024→2025 rise to US$11.5bn (2026 press release period)
growth.federal_grants: NEA arts appropriation remained flat at US$207.0m in FY2025 and FY2026 after mid-period increases in prior years

baseline_2022.market_size: US$44,995m in industry revenue (IBIS baseline figures in 2022 report)
baseline_2022.growth: IBIS baseline reported 4.4% annualized growth to a 2026 projection of about US$55.8bn; 2.45% CAGR over 2003–2021; 3.84% CAGR 2021–2027

how_it_makes_money: Live performance, exhibition, and event ticket/attendance revenue
Creative services and commission contracts (writing, acting, directing, design, visual production)
Intellectual property licensing, rights sales, and syndication
Digital monetization: paid subscriptions, memberships, ad share, tips, and tips-on-platform
Direct consumer sales and sponsorship + public/private grants
cost_structure: Core cost is creator time and project labor, often with thin margins
Variable production and touring costs (travel, staging, studio, sets, software/hardware, insurance)
Commissions, platform fees, payment processing, and distribution fees
Marketing costs (audience acquisition, social promotion, portfolio visibility)
Administrative/tax compliance overhead for independent operators (Schedule C, entity formation, accounting)
major_players: Spotify/Apple Music and major streaming ecosystems
National Endowment for the Arts (public funding channel)
current_dynamics: 2026 payroll data for NAICS 7115 are still modest and volatile, with May 2026 at 56.3k employees versus 56.9k in May 2025.
Nonemployer concentration remains very high; the 2023 Census-linked gig baseline still records over one million IAWP proprietorships.
US music demand is supported by subscription streaming growth, with RIAA reporting 106.5M paid accounts and US$6.4bn subscription revenue for 2025.
Creator platforms expanded trust-and-safety/process operations through 2025, indicating scale-up in operational footprint and governance.
whats_growing: March 2026: RIAA reported US music subscription economics continued lifting the 2025 market to US$11.5bn.
2025: RIAA 2025 mid-year reported full-format revenue growth with 105.3M premium paid subscriptions in first half.
2025: creator-platform financing layers (subscriptions, memberships, live video communities) stayed central to independent artist cashflow in public filings and platform reporting.
whats_shrinking: 2026: BLS NAICS 7115 payroll employment slipped versus May 2025 (56.9k → 56.3k).
2026: Public arts funding did not scale, with NEA appropriation at US$207.0m in FY2025 and FY2026 (no nominal increase).
2025: physical/music format shares continue to face decline pressure versus digital/subscription models.
recent_developments: 2025-09-09: RIAA mid-year reported 2025 US music revenue of US$5.6bn and 105.3M premium subscriptions.
2025-07-01: Census nonemployer context article cited IAWP with 1,043,306 individual proprietorships and US$25.4bn receipts (2023 figures used as latest official breakdown).
2026-03-16: RIAA reported US 2025 recorded-music revenue at US$11.5bn; paid subscriptions reached 106.5M accounts.
2026-03-30: Patreon Transparency Report 2026 described 2025 moderation scale (103,041 creators reviewed, 66,434 object-level actions).
2026-05 (BLS table): NAICS 7115 payrolled employment in the industry was 56.3k, down from 56.9k in May 2025.
outlook: Near term, the industry is likely to remain resilient but uneven: demand is stronger for digital discoverability and repeatable fan monetization, while traditional independent creator earnings remain exposed to high volatility, AI-generated substitute content, and non-growth in federal arts appropriations.

Gig/independent creator scale
Streaming-led demand concentration within recorded arts
Grant and philanthropy dependence for noncommercial production

Hybridized revenue stacks across live, physical, and direct-to-fan channels
one_sentence: In 2026, US performers and creative artists remain a high-variance, low-barrier sector with flat-to-frail payroll growth, a large nonemployer base, and rising digital-subscription share in music monetization.

title: Perfume & Fragrance Manufacturing
one_liner: A small, concentrated U.S. manufacturing niche where premium fragrance demand is growing, but domestic plants remain highly exposed to imported materials and foreign brand-led demand.
overview: The U.S. perfume market is still relatively small versus retail peers, yet strong category momentum in 2024 and into 2025 has supported manufacturer and ingredient supplier demand. U.S. official trade data show persistent import concentration: in 2024, perfume and toilet waters imports were US$5,560.24M, while exports were US$2,074.69M. The latest IBIS baseline history shows a recovery path from 2021 through the forecast window, and 2025-2026 behavior is now shaped by higher input-cost pressure, faster online experimentation, and continued premium category leadership.

key_stats.market_size: US$13,041.7M in 2024 (U.S. perfume market, Grand View Research)
key_stats.growth: US$17,179.1M projected in 2030; 4.7% CAGR from 2025 to 2030

baseline_2022.market_size: US$3,111.9M (2022 estimated, inferred from IBISWorld 2021 manufacturing base of US$3,047.0M and IBISWorld 2021–26 projected 1.9% CAGR)
baseline_2022.growth: 2021-2026 baseline trajectory: +1.9% CAGR (IBISWorld)

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturing and packaging of finished perfumes, toilet waters, and fragrance concentrates sold as proprietary products into prestige and mass channels.
B2B custom formula development and contract manufacturing for beauty and cosmetics groups (including luxury fashion and beauty brands).
Supply of fragrance ingredients/ingredients blends and branded ingredient-related solutions to perfume and consumer-goods makers.
Premium product mix monetization through higher-margin concentration ranges (EDP/Fragrance oils), travel-size and trial formats, and private-label/private-brand partnerships.
Digital channel growth via direct e-commerce and omnichannel distribution support for personalization and faster launch cycles.
cost_structure: High cost of key scent chemicals, botanicals, and specialty inputs sourced through import-reliant supply chains.
Regulatory compliance and testing costs for quality, labeling, and safety requirements in multiple geographies.
Substantial R&D spend for new accords, naturalization, stability, and sensory differentiation.
Packaging, bottling, logistics, and warehousing costs, including duty-sensitive and tariff-sensitive imported components.
Commercial spend concentrated in marketing, retail partnerships, influencer-led demand generation, and digital sales infrastructure.
major_players: LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton (perfume and beauty fragrance portfolio)
current_dynamics: 2024 U.S. perfume demand remained structurally supportive, with perfume and fragrance cited as the fastest-growing beauty category in both prestige and mass contexts by U.S. market data releases.
U.S. imports of HS 330300 (perfumes and toilet waters) were US$5,560.24M in 2024, while exports were US$2,074.69M, implying continued dependence on inbound ingredient/product flows.
Franchise concentration by geography remains evident: France, Spain, and Italy were the top U.S. source countries for imported perfumes and toilet waters in 2024.
Digital and social-commerce dynamics (personalization, virtual discovery, TikTok-led influence) are strengthening direct reach and new product tests in 2025.
whats_growing: Premium fragrance segment strength in the U.S. (largest segment and fastest-growing segment in 2024 according to U.S. market outlook data).
E-commerce and digitally assisted discovery for fragrance (personalized recommendations, virtual beauty workflows) in 2025 and beyond.
Demand for cleaner, natural, and story-led ingredients as brands reposition formulations.
Growth of smaller-format and trial-oriented SKUs within prestige and women’s categories as friction points in purchase frequency drop.
whats_shrinking: Import-intensive profitability: tariff and input cost pressure increased in 2025, leading to margin compression and passing-through pressure.
Mass-market fragrance growth is less reliable versus premium-led demand than earlier years.
Dependence on a narrow set of sourcing geographies and high-profile ingredient routes creates concentration risk.
recent_developments: 2025-02-12: Circana reported U.S. beauty sales rose and fragrance was the fastest-growing category (12% in prestige in 2024).
2025: DSM-Firmenich’s 2025 outlook commentary cited tariff pressure, distribution shifts, and ongoing strong demand for sustainable products.
2025-10-17: IFF announced a full settlement of direct-purchaser fragrance class actions in the U.S.
2025-11-17: U.S. court granted preliminary approval of the IFF settlement and a US$26M fund was set to resolve direct-purchaser claims.
2026-01-27: IFF disclosed a new indirect-purchaser/class action complaint was filed in New Jersey.
2026-02-05: IFF reported receiving DOJ notice of closure of its antitrust investigation; 2026-02-27 filing of FY2025 10-K.
outlook: The sector is positioned for continued moderate growth through 2026-2030, with market expansion strongest in premium fragrance and digital-first shopping journeys. Trade exposure and supplier concentration remain key constraints, so U.S. manufacturers that deepen formulation IP, direct-to-consumer pathways, and cost-efficient sourcing will likely outperform.
themes: Premiumization over volume-led pricing
Digital personalization and social-driven fragrance discovery
Natural/clean formulation narratives
Imports and tariff sensitivity in raw materials
Regulatory and litigation scrutiny in fragrance supply and claims
Resilient discretionary demand supported by affordable-luxury positioning
one_sentence: The U.S. perfume and fragrance manufacturing base is modest in size but benefiting from resilient fragrance demand, with growth increasingly driven by premiumization, digital selling models, and natural-scent positioning.

title: Perfume & Fragrance Stores
one_liner: A mature U.S. specialty retail segment where fragrance remains resilient but faces flat to low-growth demand and accelerating channel competition from e-commerce.
overview: The US perfume and fragrance stores segment (NAICS 446120) covers brick-and-mortar specialty perfume and beauty fragrance sellers and related omnichannel formats. Current market data show modest 2025 sales expansion and near-term growth uncertainty as operators rebalance toward off-mall footprints, higher productivity stores, and more digital-first assortment, discovery, and fulfillment models.
how_it_makes_money: Operators generate revenue from direct sale of perfumes, colognes, and adjacent fragrance formats through physical stores and e-commerce channels, with revenue mix often supporting beauty categories and promotional bundles. In leading specialists, fragrance is a meaningful category contributor; Ulta Beauty reported fragrance at 13% of net sales in 2025.

primary_costs: Occupancy and rent burden (noted as a significant line item alongside COGS in public beauty retailers)
Store operating payroll and logistics, including fulfillment and omnichannel costs
Promotions, marketing, and inventory investments to protect margin in high-competition categories
margin_pressure: High category substitutability and heavy price comparison behavior
Higher fixed cost exposure from retail footprint commitments
Need to balance full-price assortment with markdowns to sustain conversion

Digital channels continue to outpace in-store growth in beauty overall, reinforcing omnichannel retail expectations for fragrance discovery, refill, and replenishment.
Industry operators are shifting store mix toward off-mall or experiential formats as mall sensitivity increases.
whats_growing: US fragrance category growth remained strong in 2025 in mass and prestige channels (Circana: 15% and 5% respectively).
Online beauty purchasing behavior remains a structural expansion source and is materially faster than in-store growth.
Large fragrance-led retailers are investing in consumer-first omnichannel models and marketplace expansion.
High-income and niche/perfume discovery demand continues to support premium fragrance experimentation.
whats_shrinking: Industry-wide sectoral output growth was only 0.9% in 2025, indicating a low-growth environment.
U.S. full-year guidance from leading fragrance-adjacent chains shows cautious or declining growth assumptions into 2026.
Mall-dependent formats face sustained pressure, pushing closures/repositioning toward off-mall or digitally integrated points of sale.

outlook: The segment is likely to stay in a mature, low-growth regime through 2026, with selective upside for operators that improve destination-store density, optimize location mix, and use analytics-driven assortment to win repeat online demand without over-investing in low-productivity square footage.

Omnichannel pricing and promotional tension between full-line and private-label assortment

Operational focus on occupancy, inventory turns, and productivity gains

title: Personal Injury Lawyers & Attorneys
one_liner: The U.S. personal injury bar remains a lead-driven, contingency-fee market with steady talent growth but mixed demand signals from changing accident and safety trends.
overview: US personal injury legal services sit within broader office-of-lawyer activity and are supported by high personal injury awareness and case sourcing competition. 2024 U.S. traffic safety and 2024 workplace fatality declines indicate a softer claim-creation backdrop in parts of the accident pipeline, but legal-advertising intensity and 2025 labor expansion show demand pressure persists. 2025 data also show lawyer supply and legal-occupation earnings remain elevated, reinforcing the sector’s labor- and marketing-cost intensity.

market_size.notes: Derived from 2021 IBIS baseline value ($41.5B) using reported 2021 growth of +1.8% in 2021 profile language.

growth.notes: IBIS profile cited 2021 growth at 1.8% and 2025 revenue at ~$41.5B base in provided baseline file.

how_it_makes_money: Case-based contingency fees remain the core revenue engine in personal injury litigation.
Lead sourcing and conversion from legal advertising, referral portals, and lead-generation networks drive case volume.
Additional revenue is reinforced by case management service fees, cost reimbursements, and settlement-related participation.

cost_structure.notes: 2025 OEWS shows high legal occupation wage levels (lawyer mean ~$185,840/year), with legal support occupations also a major payroll component.
Legal services advertising was $2.5B in 2024, indicating high client acquisition spend and rising per-unit ad costs even as ad counts shifted.
2022 office-of-lawyers expenses of $228.8B vs revenue $343.0B imply ~66.7% documented operating expense ratio in Census-based official accounts.

major_players: Legal Brand Marketing (lead generation platform model)
current_dynamics: Attorney labor markets remain broad-based in 2025 while case-flow competition intensifies through scale in digital lead channels.
Ad economics are increasingly cost-per-lead sensitive: legal advertising spend rose ~39% from 2020 to 2024 while ad counts declined overall.
Injury sourcing is mixed: workplace and motor-vehicle fatality indicators softened in 2024, while legal service delivery infrastructure stayed expansionary.
whats_growing: 2025 legal-service workforce: 1,354.9k jobs in NAICS 5411.
2025 legal occupation workforce: 872k full-time wage-and-salary lawyers.
Brand-led personal-injury marketing concentration (top advertisers and aggregation platforms) remains strong.
whats_shrinking: NHTSA-estimated traffic fatalities: 2024 down 3.8% vs 2023.
BLS worker fatal injuries: 2024 total 5,070, down 4.0% vs 2023.
Raw ad quantity in legal services moved lower with higher spend, indicating margin pressure on inefficient lead channels.
recent_developments: 2025-04-08: NHTSA estimated 39,345 US traffic fatalities in 2024, down 3.8% from 40,901 in 2023.
2025-04-08: NHTSA/FHWA preliminary 2024 showed fatalities per 100M miles at 1.20 (lowest since 2019 but above pre-COVID average).
2026-04-28: BLS reported 5,070 workplace fatalities in 2024, a 4.0% drop from 5,283 in 2023; construction deaths in private sector were 1,034 in 2024.
2026-01-31: Census/FRED reported offices-of-lawyers 2022 revenue of $343,016M and expenses of $228,778M.
2026-01-28: FRED CPS table reported 872k employed full-time wage-and-salary lawyers in 2025.
outlook: For 2025–2026, the segment should stay resilient with legal-market tailwinds from sustained marketing intensity and stable legal labor supply, but growth is likely uneven as traditional motor-vehicle and occupational claim generation is decelerating versus prior years.
themes: Lead generation concentration and ad-price inflation
Talent and wage inflation within legal services
Marketing-led customer acquisition
Potential demand normalization from improving road and workplace safety metrics
Scale advantages for firms with strong brand and referral infrastructure
one_sentence: Personal injury lawyers remain concentrated around large national firms and aggressive digital/client acquisition channels, while 2025 labor and wage data suggest the legal services workforce is expanding even as some traditional injury-generating channels cool.

title: Personal Protective Equipment Manufacturing
one_liner: US PPE manufacturers are shifting from pandemic surge growth to sustained, policy-driven domestic supply and safety compliance demand.
overview: The 2022 IBIS baseline showed a maturing US PPE manufacturing industry with a 2022 revenue base of USD 7.004 billion and post-pandemic demand elevated across healthcare, construction, and industrial sectors. Current 2025–2026 signals indicate continued expansion in total PPE demand, stronger emphasis on reliable stockpiling and domestic sourcing, and accelerating product and regulatory sophistication around respiratory protection, including federal guidance updates and healthcare policy initiatives.

market_size.source_anchor: US PPE market size estimated by Mordor for 2026

baseline_2022.ibis_note: IBISWorld baseline reported USD 7.0B revenue in 2022 and a projected move toward USD 8.4B by 2027.

how_it_makes_money: Sell PPE by product line to safety-regulated buyer groups in construction, industrial manufacturing, mining, logistics, and healthcare.
Generate recurring revenue from consumable products (respirators, masks, gloves, filters, replacements) with frequent replenishment cycles.
Capture premiums through higher-specification gear for healthcare infection control, chemical/industrial use, and construction fall protection.
Grow share through supplier consolidation and strategic distribution into hospital and industrial procurement channels.

cost_structure.materials: Plastics/resins remain the dominant input category; polypropylene-linked respirator and protective product costs are sensitive to raw-material pricing.
cost_structure.labor: Wages and compliance workloads rise with product complexity, fit-testing support, documentation, and audit-readiness.
cost_structure.regulatory_quality: NIOSH/OSHA compliance drives testing, certification maintenance, and program support, increasing quality and documentation cost.
cost_structure.scale_and_supply: Automation and near-shoring reduce unit costs in standardized segments, while custom or smart PPE remains margin-supportive.
cost_structure.inventory_burden: Stockpile-oriented demand increases working-capital needs and shelf-life/rotation management requirements.

current_dynamics: US PPE demand remains anchored by healthcare and industrial compliance needs rather than purely emergency buying cycles.
Regulatory updates in 2025–2026 are reshaping respiratory-program expectations, especially around medical evaluations and premarket policy.
Domestic procurement policy is becoming a commercial differentiator as federal agencies evaluate hospital-level incentives and designations for US-made sourcing.
Stockpiling and shelf-life management practices are becoming part of buyer decision criteria after repeated multi-year guidance updates.
Competition is splitting between lower-cost commoditized imports and quality-focused domestic players with stronger regulatory credibility.
whats_growing: US PPE market rising from USD 15.6 billion in 2025 to USD 17.36 billion in 2026.
Respiratory protection projected as the fastest-growing category (13.38% CAGR, 2026-2031).
Smart/connected PPE and higher-spec products gaining share under digital and readiness use cases.
Healthcare and life-sciences demand share remains high, with hospital-led procurement influence (2025).
Domestic-source policy design work increasing demand visibility for US-compliant and traceable suppliers.
whats_shrinking: COVID-era emergency spikes in PPE purchasing have cooled versus 2020 peaks.
Import-competitive basic products face heavier pressure where price is the only deciding factor.
Hospital overstock carried from late-2020s peak periods is constraining near-term reorder tempo in some channels.
Commoditized single-use categories face margin pressure from oversupply of low-cost alternatives.
recent_developments: 2025-07-01: OSHA published a proposed rule to amend medical-evaluation requirements in respiratory-protection-related standards (NPRM, 90 FR 28463).
2025-11-20: CDC NIOSH posted stockpile guidance on respirator shelf-life and rotation management.
2025-11: MSA announced a USD 200 million acquisition of M&C TechGroup (strategic expansion into risk and gas-detection adjacent solutions).
2025-11: Honeywell announced PPE portfolio divestiture for USD 1.33 billion, with major PPE assets transferred to Protective Industrial Products.
2026-01-29: CMS ANPRM signaled policy options to promote domestic PPE procurement and a possible Secure American Medical Supplies designation.
2026-04-20: FDA published draft guidance for certain NIOSH-approved air-purifying respirators (non-binding, comment period open).
outlook: The 2026–2027 outlook is one of moderated but durable growth as healthcare, construction, and industrial safety programs continue replacing and refreshing PPE portfolios while policy tilts toward domestic capacity and resilience. Baseline momentum from 2022 remains relevant, but the near-term driver is no longer only pandemic replacement demand; it is now compliance reliability, stockpile readiness, and procurement policy clarity.
themes: Domestic resilience and security-focused sourcing
Respiratory protection as the fastest-growing segment
Regulatory modernization around RPP and respirator compliance
Strategic consolidation and reconfiguration of product portfolios
Shift from pure volume buying to quality/traceability/stockpile reliability
Smart PPE and connected safety ecosystems
one_sentence: The US PPE manufacturing market is at USD 17.36 billion in 2026 and is expected to compound at 11.28% through 2031 under a mixed commercial and resilience-driven demand mix.

title: Personal Trainers
one_liner: Demand for U.S. personal trainers is being supported by stronger fitness-facility engagement, rising health risk profiles, and hybrid coaching models.
overview: The U.S. personal training industry sits inside the broader health and fitness services demand chain, where access and retention are increasingly tied to recurring facility habits, preventive health behavior, and convenience-led delivery. IBISWorld’s 2025 report places industry size at $11.9bn in 2026 and describes a highly fragmented market without dominant operators, while HFA shows 2025 as a membership and engagement record year for fitness facilities. Demand signals are reinforced by persistent obesity and overweight prevalence from CDC data, yet utilization is shifting toward value-protected formats (small group, online coaching, in-home services) and higher-service outcomes.

key_stats.market_size: $11.9bn (2026, IBISWorld July 2025 report)
key_stats.growth: Revenue CAGR +8.2% between 2020 and 2025 (IBISWorld); 81M facility members in 2025, +5.2% vs 2024 (HFA April 2026)
key_stats.facility_engagement: ~7.0B facility visits in 2025 and 184,043 visits per location (+4.2% YoY in 2025) (HFA FIT Tracker)
key_stats.labor: 12% projected employment growth for fitness trainers and instructors from 2024 to 2034; 370,100 workers in 2024 (BLS, OOH)

baseline_2022.market_size: $13.2bn (derived from baseline 2021 level $12.9bn with +2.2% uplift signal in baseline report)
baseline_2022.growth: +2.2% implied year-on-year baseline-growth signal (from 2021 IBISWorld baseline period)

how_it_makes_money: Industry revenue is primarily earned through one-on-one coaching and small-group sessions, with additional revenue from in-home training, online coaching, and allied services such as nutrition, mobility/rehab support, and retention-focused packaged programs. In practice, operators increasingly monetize by combining session coaching with recurring programs, tiered memberships, and wellness add-ons.
cost_structure: Labour is the largest variable cost (trainer time and certifications), followed by facility-related costs (rent, lease-to-serve), insurance/compliance, marketing, and digital stack costs. Self-employed and in-home models reduce fixed overhead, while facility-employed models carry higher fixed costs but gain higher utilization through member flow, with wage pressure supported by median pay near $46,180 in 2024 (BLS).
current_dynamics: The sector benefits from a broader fitness revival: HFA’s 2026 report shows 81M US members in 2025 and 26.1% population penetration (6+), while 2025 research reports higher participation in PT and small-group formats among gym users. At the same time, session economics are changing—member activity is broader but average PT session frequency is lower than 2019—so trainers are shifting toward specialization, retention systems, and hybrid delivery. Demand remains positively correlated with obesity/overweight trends and aging/active-living demographics.
whats_growing: 2025: 81M US facility members; +5.2% YoY vs 2024 (HFA).
2025: Average visits rose to ~184,043 per location, up 4.2% (HFA FIT Tracker).
2024: 22.6% of members used personal trainers; 32.3% used small-group training (HFA).
2024-2025: Personal trainers increasingly offering nutrition, wellness, and holistic support alongside training.
2026: NASM survey shows rising trainer adoption of AI in weekly workflow (45%), supporting hybrid operating models.
2021-2023: Adult obesity remains high at 40.3% (CDC), sustaining demand for behavioral health coaching.
whats_shrinking: 2024: Average PT sessions per member fell to 21 from 28 in 2019 (HFA).
2025: Luxury facility average visits per location declined 2.0% versus prior-year quarter profile in HFA’s 2025 data.
2025: Session-intensity and consumer attention are spread across group, at-home, and app-assisted delivery, reducing pure hour-for-hour PT intensity.
2025-2026: Competitive intensity remains high with no company >5% share in IBISWorld, increasing price pressure on standard 1:1 offerings.
2025: Session models increasingly commoditize at lower price points in high-volume markets, raising pressure on unspecialized providers.
recent_developments: 2026-04-09: HFA reported 81M Americans held fitness facility memberships in 2025, up 5.2% from 2024.
2026: HFA Fitness Industry Traffic data showed gyms/studios averaging 184,043 visits per location in 2025 (+4.2% YoY).
2024-2025: HFA found 22.6% of members worked with personal trainers in 2024 and small-group participation reached 32.3%.
2024-2026: BLS OOH projects exercise trainers/group fitness instructors at +12% growth from 2024–2034 (about 74,200 annual openings).
2024-2023: CDC NCHS estimates adults age 20+ obesity at 40.3% and severe obesity at 9.4%; CDC child/adolescent obesity remains elevated at 21.1%.
2026: Planet Fitness reported +900,000 Q1 members and confirmed >20M total members.
outlook: Demand through 2026 is likely to remain positive, driven by persistent obesity and aging-related active-health demand and high facility engagement, while operator profitability depends on moving from commodity sessions to premiumized niches (rehabilitation, longevity, sports specialization, preventive-care-linked coaching) and tighter operational systems.
themes: Hybrid in-person + digital coaching
Aging wellness demand
Niche specialization (rehab, sport, chronic-condition fitness)
Session-pack value conversion
AI-enabled coaching workflows
Low share concentration and local consolidation
