Walgreens Boots Alliance (chain model; relevant competitive pressure)
current_dynamics: Independent networks remain vital, while large chains and mass merchants continue to pressure retail prices in adjacent channels.
Part D/Medicare reimbursement rules and MFP/MTP workflows in 2026 are shaping frontline cash flow and service mix.
Clinical and preventive-care positioning (vaccination, MTM, screening) is becoming more important than pure dispensing scale.
whats_growing: 2025-2026: Preventive and clinical service intensity increased, with immunization and care management offerings becoming key differentiation at community pharmacies.
2025: The NCPA report indicates independent pharmacies are maintaining high relevance despite closures, with 93% offering flu immunizations and most offering broader medication-care services.
2025: US older-population growth continued (65+ at 61.2 million in 2024 and rising), supporting chronic medication demand over the medium term.
2025: Prescription spend accelerated (2025 drug spending up 12.7%), keeping dispense volumes elevated versus earlier normalization years.
whats_shrinking: 2024→2025: Independent pharmacy location count declined from 18,984 to 18,960 before 2026 rebound, showing continuing churn in undercapitalized operators.
Industry-wide competition from chains and big-box formats remains high, limiting basket expansion and local pricing power.
Reimbursement-to-cost gaps for generic acquisition and dispensing economics persist, creating margin compression despite revenue growth.
Patient access pressure in “pharmacy-desert” neighborhoods increases operating risk and reputational scrutiny even as some stores remain profitable.
recent_developments: 2025-10-19: NCPA reported independent community pharmacies at 18,960 locations (down from 18,984 in June 2024) and a $103 billion independent marketplace.
2025-10-19: NCPA also reported over half of prescriptions in that segment are covered by Medicare Part D and Medicaid combined, signaling dependence on managed programs.
2026-02-10: PCMA reported independent pharmacy locations rose by 67 between 2025 and 2026.
2026-04-30: ASHP reported 2025 prescription drug spending up 12.7% to $915.2 billion and projected 2026 spending to exceed $1 trillion.
2025-06-25: NCPA highlighted that roughly 1 in 8 US neighborhoods are pharmacy shortage areas.
2025-06-25: NCPA member alert detailed 2026 Part D MFP rollout (10 initial negotiated drugs, MTF enrollment, and refund timing) and associated operational pressure.
outlook: The 2026–2028 outlook is one of structural duality: volume drivers remain strong from age and utilization trends, while operating margins remain vulnerable to contract mechanics and reimbursement lag. Franchise operators that pair dispensing with higher-value services and tighter cost controls should outperform pure price-based competitors, with market leadership likely shifting toward networks that absorb Part D contract volatility more efficiently.
themes: Aging demographic demand versus reimbursement squeeze
PBM settlement terms and MTF implementation risk
Clinical-service migration from pure retail dispensing
Store-density decline and pharmacy-desert sensitivity
Independents as access providers despite scale disadvantages
one_sentence: The industry is stable at low-single-digit growth in 2026, with demand supported by older age demographics and higher prescription spending, while PBM contract terms and Part D reimbursement mechanics cap profitability.

title: Pharmacy Benefit Management
one_liner: PBMs in 2026 continue to be the policy-heavy, high-concentration rail between payers and pharmacies, with large portions of U.S. prescription-volume still routed through a few dominant operators.
overview: The industry provides third-party administration of prescription drug benefits for commercial plans, employers, Medicare Part D, Medicare Advantage and Medicaid-related plans through claim adjudication, formulary management, pharmacy networks, rebate negotiation, and specialty workflow. Demand is supported by an insured U.S. population with a major chronic-care burden and high drug utilization, while growth is increasingly shaped by policy constraints on PBM compensation, reporting, and pass-through behavior.

notes.2022_estimation_basis: Estimated from 2021 baseline $457.8B and historical growth path used in provided industry baseline.

baseline_2022.reference: provided IBIS-style baseline file and 2021 base value

how_it_makes_money: Claims administration and adjudication fees paid by employers/insurers.
Network and dispensing economics from pharmacy and specialty fulfillment channels.
Rebate and pricing-discount negotiation tied to formularies and preferred drug tiers.
Fee-based advisory and compliance services tied to plan administration and provider contracting.
cost_structure: High fixed cost in claims-processing and data infrastructure to support near-real-time benefit checks.
Clinical and pharmacy-network operating costs (reimbursement setting, formulary updates, provider relations).
Regulatory and legal costs from ERISA, Part D, and disclosure/audit readiness.
Margin pressure from rebate/discount pressure in high-volume brand and specialty categories.
current_dynamics: 2025 data show high concentration (Top 3 processed about 80% of equivalent claims) while policy has shifted toward mandatory transparency and auditability through CAA 2026 and related DOL PBM fee-disclosure action. At the same time, CMS reports 2026 MA/Part D premium moderation (MA average from $16.40 in 2025 to $14.00 in 2026; standalone Part D from $38.31 to $34.50), supporting volume continuity for PBM-administered plans.
whats_growing: 2025–2026: Big-three processing share is still high, but independent PBMs are gaining some business according to recent PBM industry reporting.
2026: Specialty and chronic-care pharmacy workflow remains elevated, supporting demand for benefit design, adherence, and specialty channel management.
2025–2026: Federal scrutiny and disclosure rights are expanding, creating demand for contract redesign, analytics, and audit-ready reporting services.
whats_shrinking: 2025–2026: Gross-to-net rebate growth in brand-name channels has slowed, reducing easy spread between list/net economics.
Price opacity-based business practices are under tighter legal constraints (revenue capture from opaque compensation structures under pressure).
Consolidation among insurers/plan channels is creating stronger counterparty bargaining power in some large employer and group markets.
recent_developments: 2026-01-30: DOL EBSA published the PBM fee disclosure proposed rule (FR 91 FR 4348), requiring compensation transparency for providers serving ERISA plans.
2026-02-03: H.R.7148 became Public Law No. 119-75 (CAA 2026), adding PBM rebate pass-through, reporting, and fiduciary protections.
2026-03-02: DOL extended the PBM disclosure rule comment period to 2026-04-15 and tied it to CAA 2026 changes.
2026-02 (FTC): FTC announced a settlement with Express Scripts requiring PBM business-practice changes aimed at greater transparency and lower OOP drug costs.
2025-04-07: CMS finalized CY 2025 Part D redesign instructions, changing patient cost-sharing structure and defining new rebate/money-flow mechanics under IRA implementation.
outlook: Demand should remain steady-to-grow as Rx utilization rises, but industry economics are likely to bifurcate: high-volume incumbents keep scale advantages while the most profitable behaviors shift toward transparent, contractized rebate remittance and service-fee models. Short term, policy-induced contract redesign is likely to outweigh purely utilization-led growth.
themes: Concentration vs. transparency reform
Employer self-insured governance pressure
Prescription volume concentration in chronic and specialty drugs
Digital claims and pharmacy-network scalability
Rebate economics restructuring
one_sentence: In 2026, the PBM model remains demand-positive as prescription-drug utilization and spending stay high (CMS projects retail prescription spending at $518.7B in 2025 after $467.0B in 2024), but margin and contract risk are rising under the new rebate-disclosure and fiduciary-audit regime.

title: Photofinishing in the US
one_liner: U.S. photofinishing is a shrinking physical-print market where volume is pressured by smartphones and social media, while personalized photo goods and online ordering remain the durable growth pockets.
overview: The US photofinishing industry has moved from a broad consumer photo-processing model toward a narrower workflow driven by smartphones, social sharing, and convenience channels. Core film and basic print processing are structurally weaker, while personalized products (photo books, canvases, mugs, and housewares) and fulfillment reliability are better at holding value. Large retailers and online service providers dominate distribution and pricing pressure, making scale and specialization the main levers for survival.

key_stats.growth: -0.9% annualized (2021–2026 projected)

Event and family-moment bundles (weddings, portraits, graduation packages)
Outsourced fulfillment/print-to-door and quick turnaround premium services

Labor including digital workflow operators, color management, and customer support

Distribution and fulfillment costs, especially shipping and last-mile handling
Footprint costs for stores or kiosks where in-person capture/print still happens

Industry labor-hour data show contraction (11.464m hours in 2022 to 8.828m hours in 2025), and IBIS-style business-level tracking shows 2025 at 5,476 firms with -0.4% annual growth, consistent with continued consolidation and weaker margins in commodity workflows.
whats_growing: Personalized and premium photo merchandise formats
Online direct ordering and at-home-to-kiosk digital workflows
Event-driven commemorative orders rather than routine daily snapshots
whats_shrinking: Traditional low-value film and basic print volume
Independent standalone photofinishing counters as volume centralizes
Commodity 4x6 and single-use transactional jobs with high price sensitivity

outlook: Through 2026, the market is likely to keep contracting in core print volume, but firms that shift from commodity processing to personalization, speed, and partner distribution should preserve the highest margins. Further consolidation is likely as small operators lose scale against national chains and online platforms.

Channel shift from physical counters to omnichannel digital ordering
Premiumization through personalized photo goods
Consolidation around low-margin price competition
Operational thinning: fewer establishments and lower labor intensity
one_sentence: Photofinishing demand in 2025–2026 is lower in volume but more selective, with value concentrated in premium merchandise, event-related products, and digital-to-print conversion through large retail and online platforms.

title: Photography in the US
one_liner: The U.S. photography market remains a mature, low-growth services industry in 2025–2026, with demand anchored by weddings and commercial image production while DIY and AI tools keep pressure on commodity work.
overview: After the pandemic reset, the industry continues to run with uneven recovery: portrait and event operators still depend on discretionary consumer spending, while commercial photography is supported by advertising and branding demand. NAICS 541921 (portrait photography services) is still the most visible labor-heavy segment and had 53.3K jobs in 2025 after recovering from 39.3K in 2020. At the same time, wedding pricing data still shows a clear willingness to pay for premium photo services, even as smartphones and AI-driven workflows reduce barriers for basic capture and editing.

key_stats.market_size: $10,087M total photography industry revenue (2022 baseline); NAICS 541921 sectoral output $9,021.19M (2022); NAICS 541921 employment 53.3K (2025)
key_stats.growth: IBISWorld baseline projection: +0.19% annualized 2022–2028; BLS Occupational Outlook for photographers: +2% 2024–2034 (151,200→154,000 projected).

baseline_2022.growth: +0.19% annualized to 2028 (from 2022 base)
baseline_2022.notes: 2022 IBISWorld baseline with 52.7% consumer share and 47.3% commercial mix.

how_it_makes_money: Primary revenue is from service delivery (wedding, family portrait, school, commercial shoots), packaging and bundling (engagement sessions, albums, digital assets), retouching and delivery tiers, and occasional licensing/stock and product sales; recurring revenue is increasingly linked to memberships, education, and software-enabled workflows.
cost_structure: Labor is the largest cost because each assignment requires capture + studio time + post-production. Variable costs include travel, event logistics, assistants, model/venue coordination, and digital delivery. Fixed/ongoing costs include high-end camera/mirrorless systems, lighting kits, editing workstations, insurance, software licensing (including AI and cloud), and professional liability/marketing. WeddingWire shows operators commonly include equipment, payroll, business expenses, and insurance in package pricing, indicating these remain embedded overhead.
current_dynamics: Demand remains segmented: weddings and portrait sessions still fund premium pricing, while higher-frequency volume work faces stronger price pressure from DIY alternatives. Smartphone ownership reached near-ubiquity, which supports easy in-house capture and keeps consumer expectations of speed high. AI-assisted creative tools are being integrated into production pipelines and education channels, increasing productivity for active studios but also lowering entry barriers for non-professional creators.
whats_growing: 2026 data shows continued consumer willingness to pay for wedding photography, with The Knot reporting average US professional wedding photographer cost around $3,000 (2025 cohort, 10,474 couples).
Nonemployer participation remains structurally high in the business, consistent with IBISLong-established entry patterns and freelance-oriented supply.
Tool-led workflows are expanding: Adobe announced conversational AI-driven image workflows and portfolio-level editing upgrades in 2026.
Professional education and community monetization is expanding (PPA PhotoVision launched in 2025 with 2,500+ videos and 1,700+ articles).
whats_shrinking: 2025 portrait-employment in NAICS 541921 slipped from 54.3K (2024) to 53.3K (2025), reflecting tighter pricing conditions in high-volume segments.
Wedding and special-event growth is indirectly constrained by demographic softness: CDC reports births fell 1% in 2025 to 3,606,400.
Smartphone saturation in 2025 (97–99% cellphone ownership; 91–97% smartphone ownership by age group and near-universal ownership in many cohorts) supports substitution at lower-price tiers.
Premium photography remains vulnerable to AI-generated or heavily edited substitutes in generic imagery use cases.
recent_developments: 2025-11-03: PPA launched PhotoVision, stating it includes 2,500+ videos and 1,700+ articles.
2025-11-03: PPA added paid/nonmember subscription access for PhotoVision education and business operations content.
2026-03-10: Adobe announced AI Assistant and new AI editing capabilities in Photoshop/Firefly, increasing workflow automation in image production.
2026-04-09: CDC reported US births declined 1% in 2025 to 3,606,400, a demand proxy for family-event photography volume.
2026-06-03: FRED updated NAICS 541921 employment (portrait photography) to 53.3K jobs for 2025.
2026-05-08 (from The Knot update): average professional wedding photographer fee remains $3,000 in 2025 methodology sample.
outlook: For 2026–2028, market behavior is likely to remain low- to mid-single-digit unless wedding conversion and commercial imaging budgets stay resilient. Winners are likely firms that differentiate through niche positioning, rapid AI-assisted delivery, and premium post-production service bundles; laggards are more exposed in commodity event capture where consumers can substitute with smartphone content.
themes: Premiumization of key-demand moments (weddings/brand shoots)
AI-enabled production productivity
High-friction competitive pressure on low-value image capture
Dominance of micro/freelance operator model
Demand sensitivity to demographics and discretionary household income
one_sentence: In 2026, US photography shows a bifurcation between high-value custom work that benefits from expertise and relationship value, and low-differentiation image capture increasingly challenged by smartphone adoption.

title: Physical Therapists in the US
one_liner: Outpatient and post-acute physical therapy in the US is expanding on aging, musculoskeletal, and surgical-recovery demand while facing tight labor supply, payer pressure, and narrow reimbursement rules.
overview: US physical therapy remains a high-demand service segment driven by older adults, chronic conditions, and post-acute recovery, with care settings spread across private outpatient clinics, hospitals, home health, and long-term care. CMS remains a central determinant of effective reimbursement through therapy thresholds, telehealth scope, and audit rules, while demand in many metros now exceeds local delivery capacity during certain periods.

key_stats.market_size_note: APTA-associated workforce reporting (2026 profile) reports 312,199 licensed PTs nationwide, alongside 132,105 PT assistants.

baseline_2022.baseline_context: IBIS baseline also described pent-up post-COVID demand and 2022 revenue growth above historical levels.

how_it_makes_money: Outpatient therapy visits billed under Medicare Part B and private insurance reimbursement schedules.
Per-service and episode-based payment structures tied to functional progress, visit volume, and medically necessary care thresholds.
Commercial contracts with workers’ compensation, managed care networks, and employer-driven referral channels.
Ancillary rehabilitation services, orthopedics and pain-management support programs, and in some settings home care continuity.
cost_structure: Labor is the largest expense, including licensed PTs, PT assistants, and support staff.
Reimbursement compliance and documentation costs are elevated under therapy-site-of-service and audit rules.
Facilities, lease, and scheduling/admin systems are major fixed cost components for multi-site operators.
Clinic productivity and staffing mix management (PT vs PTA/aide split) are critical to margin preservation.
major_players: Select Medical (operates 1,917 outpatient rehabilitation clinics as of Dec 31 2025, one of the largest US operators)
ATI Physical Therapy (reported more than 850 locations across 24 states as of 2026)
Athletico Physical Therapy (national outpatient operator with multi-state network)
Encompass Health (large rehab operator with significant referral and post-acute rehabilitation influence)
Independent private practices and regional outpatient PT networks
current_dynamics: Aging and musculoskeletal burden continues to keep demand elevated even where geographic access is tight.
Workforce supply remains tight: APTA model outputs still show recurring shortage risk and high local wait pressure.
CMS therapy payment governance remains a direct margin and throughput variable through KX, PTA reimbursement, and multiple procedure rules.
Telehealth for PT remains allowed in narrow, policy-driven channels; in-person services still dominate core revenue.
whats_growing: Aging-related rehab and post-op recovery demand in outpatient and home/community settings.
Regional consolidation around larger operators that can negotiate payer terms and scale administrative systems.
Use of therapy assistants, hybrid team models, and workflow tech to expand capacity.
Demand for teleassessed and remote monitoring adjunct services in eligible programs.
whats_shrinking: High-margin purely episodic growth is muted by static visit-level reimbursement and strict therapy limits.
Standalone independent providers with thin capital reserves in tighter payer environments.
Purely manual scaling without workforce planning, especially in markets with persistent local PT shortages.

2025-12-10: APTA released 2025 workforce and income updates, reporting 2%–4% annual workforce growth and ~400,000+ PT/PTA participants plus waiting pressure for capacity.

2026-03-10: CMS Therapy Services page updated for CY 2026 rules, including KX threshold $2,480 and Telehealth/RTM updates through Dec 2027.
2026-05-22: ATI reported it operates more than 850 locations across 24 states.
outlook: The 2025–2026 outlook is constructive but disciplined: demand trend remains upward from demographics and aging-care needs, while operator profitability depends on workforce strategy, payer optimization, and compliance execution. Near-term growth is likely in clinic networks that can scale productivity without compromising quality, with persistent pressure in markets where local therapist capacity is below demand.

payer-policy sensitivity
workforce mix optimization
fragmented industry consolidation
telehealth boundaries
referral-channel competition
one_sentence: The industry is growing, but the pace is constrained by workforce retention, reimbursement governance, and operational productivity pressures in a fragmented provider landscape.

title: Physical Therapy Rehabilitation Centers
one_liner: Physical therapy and rehabilitation providers are growing with aging demand but are increasingly constrained by Medicare policy and rising labor costs.
overview: The industry remains a high-volume, fragmented healthcare segment spanning outpatient clinics, inpatient rehabilitation units, and post-acute care systems. Demand is supported by aging and chronic-condition prevalence, but profitability is sensitive to reimbursement methodology, therapy-utilization thresholds, staffing costs, and payer mix shifts between traditional Medicare, Medicare Advantage, and commercial plans.

key_stats.growth: 3.56% CAGR (2021-2026, IBIS baseline projection)

baseline_2022.growth: ~3.3% (estimated from 2021 IBIS base and 2021-2026 trajectory)

how_it_makes_money: Primary revenue comes from outpatient and inpatient rehabilitation encounters billed under CPT/HCPCS therapy services to Medicare Part B, Medicaid, commercial insurers, and self-pay, with revenue tied to visit volume, acuity mix, and reimbursement coding (including therapy assistant utilization, KX threshold compliance, and medical review risk). Ancillary sales and home/community programs can add upside but are secondary.
cost_structure: Labor and direct service delivery costs dominate: Select Medical reports cost of services at 88.5% of revenue in 2025 and major salary pressure, while U.S. Physical Therapy’s 2022 filing shows PT operating salaries at 57.7% of physical therapy operation revenue and total operating cost at 79.7% of revenue. Compliance and coding costs are rising with MPPR/MX edits, KX documentation, and audit-related overhead.
current_dynamics: Demand remains resilient from orthopedic recovery, stroke, and musculoskeletal rehab demand while clinics expand telehealth-enabled follow-up and post-acute transitions, but reimbursement and staffing headwinds are sharper than pre-2024 levels.
whats_growing: Aging population growth and post-acute rehab need are strengthening core demand.
CMS’ CY2026 policy adds RTM coding options (98979, 98984, 98985) that expand billable remote follow-up options.
Outpatient rehabilitation systems with scale are strengthening referral pipelines through orthopedic, hospital, and employer partnerships.
Large Medicare Advantage growth to 55% of eligible beneficiaries is increasing the importance of managed-care contract strategy.
whats_shrinking: Margin room is constrained by labor costs and utilization-control rules.
KX thresholds and targeted review rules limit claim leakage and increase documentation burden.
The industry remains highly competitive with price pressure and limited differentiation outside clinical outcomes and specialist service lines.
recent_developments: 2025-06-26: U.S. Census reported age 65+ population at 61.2 million, up 3.1% from 2023 to 2024.
2025-10-31: CMS issued the CY2026 PFS final rule (effective Jan 1, 2026) with separate conversion factors for APM and non-APM clinicians.
2026-06-05: KFF’s Medicare Advantage update reports 55% MA penetration (35.2 million of 64.2 million eligible beneficiaries) in 2026.
2026-02: CMS updated CY2026 therapy policy pages for new RTM therapy codes and the telehealth/salary documentation environment; CY2026 KX threshold is $2,480.
2026-02-24: CMS posted CY2026 MPPR updates to therapy billing files, indicating continued operational change pressure on same-day multi-service billing.
2025-12-07: CMS reported 23.6 million marketplace plan selections by Jan 4, 2025, reflecting continuing shifts in under-65 insurance access and cost exposure.
outlook: Short-term growth should remain positive but slower than historical highs, with clinics likely to prioritize operational efficiency, therapy assistant deployment, and payer-optimized care pathways. The next 12-18 months are likely to reward high-compliance, data-driven systems that can handle stricter therapy documentation while competing for referral share in a still-fragmented national market.
themes: Aging and chronic-care demand
Reimbursement engineering and coding compliance
Labor scarcity and compensation inflation
Telehealth/remote therapeutic monitoring expansion
Managed-care concentration and insurer consolidation
Scale-led consolidation among provider networks
one_sentence: U.S. physical therapy rehabilitation centers are expanding services across inpatient and outpatient settings while navigating tighter CMS payment rules, stronger workforce pressure, and a faster shift of Medicare beneficiaries into managed Medicare Advantage plans.

title: Piece Goods, Notions & Other Apparel Wholesaling in the US
one_liner: U.S. wholesalers that distribute piece goods, notions, and related apparel inputs to clothing manufacturers, uniform suppliers, and industrial buyers.
overview: The baseline IBIS outlook already described this NAICS 4243 market as mature and structurally pressured by imported production and in-house sourcing by apparel brands. In the 2025–2026 window, Census wholesale trade data still show continued activity in apparel-related wholesaling, while ITA/Census import data show sustained global textile and apparel inflows, which keeps price competition elevated. The result is a market where small-batch and service-led wholesalers can hold share, but price discounting remains intense and concentration remains low.

key_stats.market_size: 2026-05: $12,231 million in monthly NAICS 4243 apparel, piece goods, and notions merchant-wholesaler sales (S4243SM144NCEN, not seasonally adjusted); Jan–May 2026 5-month average was about $12,964 million per month.
key_stats.growth: 2026-04: +1.1% SA month-over-month in NAICS 4243 sales (P4243MM157SCEN); 2026-05: 12,231 < 2026-04: 12,923 (short-term pullback). 2025-06: U.S. textile import YE +15.9% and apparel import YE +7.9% in ITA report (in line with continued import pressure).
key_stats.employees: 2025: 146.2K jobs in NAICS 4243 (BLS employment series IPUGN4243W200000000).
key_stats.establishments: Profile references indicate a highly fragmented 4-digit NAICS base, with 13,318 total employer establishments for NAICS 4243.
key_stats.wage: 2026-05: average hourly earnings around $37.00 (BLS, NAICS 424300, monthly workforce snapshot).

baseline_2022.growth: -0.46% projected annualized (IBIS, 2022-2028)

how_it_makes_money: Primary revenue comes from wholesale of fabric and textile trims (thread, zippers, buttons, labels, notions), margin-driven by mix and volume across B2B customers. Most operators compete on inventory depth, delivery speed, and service bundles (small-batch support, private-label sourcing, technical assistance, and logistics proximity).
cost_structure: Labor remains a core fixed-plus-variable cost in order handling, sales, and customer servicing; inventory carrying and freight are highly variable and rise with slower inventory turns; transport and warehouse handling costs increase during peaks; small firms often use fewer automation layers while larger operators invest in digital cataloging and fulfillment tooling.
major_players: Large apparel brands and distributors with in-house sourcing/fulfillment structures that reduce third-party wholesaler dependence
Specialty accessory and fastener ecosystems that supply recurring button, zipper, and trim demand
Regional fabric and notion distributors serving CPG, uniform, and SMB apparel brands
Crowded private-market wholesaler landscape with no single dominant national winner in NAICS 4243
current_dynamics: 2025-06-09: US Census MWTS reported broad merchant-wholesaler sales growth and a still-elevated inventories/sales ratio, showing demand held in a volatile global trade backdrop.
2025-06-09: ITA reported U.S. textile imports at 109,356.4 MSME YE and apparel imports at 26,256.0 MSME YE, up 15.9% and 7.9% Y/Y respectively.
2026-05: NAICS 4243 monthly sales remained above $12B but showed month-to-month volatility (12,042 -> 12,231 in Jan and May 2026), consistent with demand shifts and customer procurement timing.
whats_growing: 2026-05: Continued short-cycle demand from smaller/SMB buyers needing small-lot or faster replenishment runs.
2025-2026: Sustained apparel- and textile-import flows support service-only wholesalers that package short-order fulfillment, substitutions, and QC support.
2026-01 to 2026-05: Demand remains resilient in niche product groups tied to uniform programs and custom trims.
whats_shrinking: 2025-2026: Import availability and tariff-differential sourcing keep landed-cost pressure high, pushing many wholesalers to defend volume rather than margin.
2026: Upstream apparel offshoring and vertical integration trends continue to bypass independent piece-goods brokers in some categories.
2026 volatility: NAICS 4243 monthly fluctuations (including a -6.1% MoM dip reported in the adjacent period before rebounding in April) indicate unstable order flow rather than stable expansion.
recent_developments: 2025-06: Census MWTS stated June 2025 apparel-related merchandising conditions were mixed, reinforcing cyclical volatility in wholesaling.
2025-06: ITA reported textile imports up sharply in 2025, with year-end imports 109,356.4 MSME (+15.9% vs prior year).
2026-05: FRED/ Census NAICS 4243 sales (not seasonally adjusted) = $12,231 million.
2026-04: NAICS 4243 sales growth (seasonally adjusted, ALFRED) = +1.1%, with 2026-03 at -1.9% and 2026-02 at +4.0%.
2026-05: BLS NAICS 4243 wage snapshot showed average hourly earnings around $37.00.
outlook: 2025–2026 suggests a slow-growth, volume-sensitive market through 2027 with weak structural recovery unless customers shift toward higher service intensity and less commoditized trim/inputs. Import competition and internalization remain the central downside risks, while selective growth is most likely in service-led and niche B2B distribution.
themes: Import-led price compression
Retail brand/wholesaler vertical integration
Fragmented, low-concentration structure
High monthly demand volatility
Service differentiation over pure commodity trading
one_sentence: The industry is stabilizing near-term on resilient niche demand, but imports and vertical integration keep long-term margins and participation under pressure.

title: Pilates & Yoga Studios
one_liner: Boutique yoga and Pilates studios are becoming healthier, more resilient businesses as active aging, retention-focused memberships, and platform-driven discovery pull demand, even as fixed costs and competition tighten margins.
overview: The U.S. Pilates & Yoga Studios market remains a niche within broader fitness, with demand increasingly supported by recovery and wellness use cases and older-adult participation. Industry structure is still fragmented versus large gym models, but platform ecosystems (booking, scheduling, CRM, and digital delivery) are reshaping how studios sell and retain customers. The category remains activity-centered and location dependent, so local density, instructor quality, and utilization discipline remain the key determinants of unit economics. In 2026, the market is mature by growth profile but not stagnant; expansion is coming from adjacent markets (regional spillover, senior-focused programming, prenatal and therapeutic positioning, and hybrid discovery channels) rather than mass category acceleration.

key_stats.market_size: ~USD 10.7 billion projected for 2026 (IBIS-based baseline projection), with ~USD 9.7 billion in 2021
key_stats.growth: ~1.9% CAGR (2021-2026, IBIS), and 2025 facility participation improved materially: 81.0 million members and 100+ million total users in U.S. fitness facilities (HFA 2026 report, 2025 activity)

baseline_2022.market_size: ~USD 9.86 billion (derived from 2021 baseline USD 9.678 billion and IBIS-projected 1.88% annual trajectory to 2026
baseline_2022.growth: ~1.9% implied annual growth in 2022-2026 baseline path

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is primarily from recurring memberships, class packages, drop-in/pass products, private sessions, and small-format add-ons (studio retail, workshops, and partnerships). Some operators also monetize through booking-platform distribution, corporate wellness channels, and lead generation referrals from marketplaces; margin is strongest when utilization is high and recurring attendance remains consistent.

fixed_costs: facility lease and occupancy tied to urban/mixed-use real estate;
specialized instructor payroll and staffing coverage by class schedule;
variable_costs: instructor commissions and staffing adjustments for peak-time classes;
guest passes, promotions, and referral marketing spend;
energy/maintenance tied to HVAC and class capacity
margin_implications: higher non-utilizing member rates compress cash flow;
platform and marketplace economics reward class frequency and retention more than one-time promotions

current_dynamics.demand: Pilates classes were reported up 28.1% in ClassPass booking trend data between 2021-2025; yoga remains one of the most widely practiced activities (17.7 million past-year participants in 2025 HFA tracking).
current_dynamics.utilization: HFA reports in 2025: 7.0B facility visits, membership penetration 26.1%, total users 33.5%, and churn improved to 7.1% with member tenure near 5 years.
current_dynamics.competition: Competition is rising from lower-cost fitness clubs and digital alternatives; consumer convenience and hybrid discovery continue to pull some demand to multi-location platforms.
technology: wearable and personalization signals are strengthening per ACSM 2026 trends;
booking platforms increasingly drive discovery and class conversion
current_dynamics.regulation: state-level fitness taxes and labor classification enforcement remain recurring headwinds for small-to-mid operators.

whats_growing: 2025-05: fitness demand broad-based recovery: 100+ million total users in U.S. fitness facilities (HFA).
2025-05: 17.7 million Americans practiced yoga in 2025 (HFA) and Pilates trend momentum remains high in booking platforms.
2025-10: ACSM 2026 report elevated older-adult programming and active-aging content to top-tier trends.
2025-11: ClassPass 2025 bookable-workout data showed strong growth in Pilates (+66% YoY) and yoga (+28% YoY).
2025-2026: Corporate wellness and data-driven membership products continue to pull users into paid studio ecosystems.
whats_shrinking: Traditional standalone cardio formats and lower-engagement formats are weakening in relative share (HFA notes continued decline in ellipticals/standalone cardio).
Platform bargaining pressure on low-margin drop-in traffic is increasing, reducing profitability for purely volume-driven operators.
Growth in pure low-cost commodity class supply in crowded markets intensifies price competition for core formats.
recent_developments: 2026-03-31: Playlist completed the $7.5B merger with EGYM, linking ClassPass, Mindbody, and smart-gym software into a larger wellness platform.

2026-03-04: Xponential’s 2025 10-K disclosed Club Pilates as the largest U.S. Pilates franchised brand, with 1,414 operational studios globally and 2,606 North America studios across the segment as of 12/31/2025.
2026-05-01: HFA released the 2026 U.S. Health & Fitness Consumer Report showing 81.0M members, 33.5% total penetration, and 7.0B facility visits in 2025.
2025-10-22: ACSM published the 2026 global fitness-trend report, placing wearable technology and older-adult programming in top trend lines.
2025-11-15: ClassPass 2025 Look Back Report showed Pilates and yoga among top global booking leaders, indicating sustained category demand through digital discovery channels.
outlook: Short term (2026-2028), category growth likely remains moderate rather than explosive, with better outcomes for operators that localize programs, raise visit frequency, and reduce churn. Winners will be studios that blend signature class design with low-cost digital acquisition, therapist-backed programming, and community retention. New openings are likely to favor under-penetrated or smaller metropolitan zones, while saturated metro markets continue to consolidate around stronger chains and platform-backed brands.
themes: Maturity with selective expansion
Active aging and therapeutic fitness
Hybrid digital discovery + in-person retention
Consolidation in platform and software layers
Utilization discipline over price discounting
Instructor talent and unit-level productivity matter most
one_sentence: U.S. Pilates & yoga operators are in a slow-growth, high-engagement phase in 2026, with demand broadening across demographics while profitability depends increasingly on utilization, premium class mix, and efficient distribution.

title: Pizza Restaurants
one_liner: US pizza remains a large, competitive QSR category where digital ordering and delivery are now central, but 2025 showed the first category-level pullback since the pandemic surge.
overview: In 2025, US pizza restaurants were estimated at 75,736 locations with category revenue near $49.5 billion, down 0.3% from 2024. Delivery and carryout remain the core demand channels, and the segment continues to be highly competitive with a strong role for digital ordering and loyalty. Chains and independents coexist, but major operators are benefiting from larger marketing and technology budgets while independents still form a significant portion of the market and require efficiency upgrades.

key_stats.growth: -0.3% in 2025 (category-level QSR pizza sales year-over-year)
key_stats.digital_preference: 64% of consumers prefer placing delivery or takeout orders digitally (2025)

how_it_makes_money.primary: Pizza sales through dine-in, carryout, and delivery in the US

how_it_makes_money.supplementary: Catering, frozen/retail add-ons, and grocery/retail extensions are cited as meaningful ancillary revenue sources
how_it_makes_money.unit_economics: Franchise royalties/fees and advertising income scale with same-store sales and net store growth in leading chains

cost_structure.labor: Labor intensity remains high, with operator-reported labor costs around 23%-28% and average hourly wage up 3.86% in 2025
cost_structure.food_and_supplies: Food basket pricing increased 2.2% in Domino's Q2 2026; ingredient and commodity inflation remains a structural pressure
cost_structure.delivery_and_technology: Operators face ongoing costs from digital channels, third-party delivery competition, and platform/loyalty investment
cost_structure.profitability_pressure: Category-level consumer pullback in 2025 and mixed chain performance increased focus on menu mix, productivity, and automation

current_dynamics: Top-4 chain positions remained unchanged in 2025: Domino's, Pizza Hut, Little Caesars, Papa John's

Expect continued consolidation around stronger digital-first concepts and selective menu/value repositioning, with independent operators increasingly dependent on operational efficiency and local differentiation.
